title: A statutory right, built in stages
subtitle: Unfair dismissal I: the ERA 1996 Part X scheme
objectives: State the structure of the unfair dismissal scheme under ERA 1996 Part X, including who qualifies and the current qualifying period
List the five potentially fair reasons for dismissal under ss 98(1)–(2) ERA 1996 and identify which party bears the burden of showing one
Apply the qualifying-period and potentially-fair-reason framework to a fact pattern, correctly identifying whether a claim can proceed and on what basis

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory core of the unfair dismissal right: the right itself, qualification, and the potentially fair reasons an employer must show

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson is almost entirely a statutory scaffold — get the structure right here and lessons 6 and 7 slot straight into it. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can list the five reasons — this lesson checks whether you can place a fact pattern into the right box.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on short scenarios asking which of the five reasons is engaged, or whether the qualifying period is even met: read for the threshold facts, not just the headline reason.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and learn the two-year qualifying period and the five reasons as a fixed list before moving on — Lesson 6 assumes you can recite both without hesitation.

overview.hook: Two employees are dismissed on the same day, for what looks like the same reason. One can bring an unfair dismissal claim. The other cannot even get through the door of the employment tribunal on this ground — not because their dismissal was any fairer, but because of a single fact that has nothing to do with fairness at all: how long they had worked there. This lesson is about the statutory gate that decides who gets to ask the fairness question in the first place, and what the employer then has to show once someone is through it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. This lesson teaches the qualifying period and framework currently in force: a two-year continuous service requirement before the general right to claim unfair dismissal arises. The Employment Rights Act 2025 will reduce this qualifying period to six months, but that change does not commence until 1 January 2027 and is not yet in force — it is covered in full, as prospective reform, in Lesson 15. Until commencement, the two-year period taught here remains the operative law.

parts.heading: A right you have to qualify for
parts.voice: structural — sets out the gateway before the substance
body: Unfair dismissal is a creature of statute, not the common law you met in Lesson 4. It exists because Parliament decided that 'the contract was honoured' is too low a bar for how an employer should be allowed to end someone's job — and it built an entirely separate right, with its own qualifying conditions, its own tribunal forum, and its own remedies, sitting in Part X of the Employment Rights Act 1996.

Section 94 ERA 1996 creates the right itself: an employee has the right not to be unfairly dismissed by their employer. But s 94 is not a free-standing right available to everyone from day one. As currently in force, s 108 ERA 1996 requires the employee to have two years' continuous employment with the employer before the general right to claim arises. Fall short of two years, and — subject to the automatically unfair categories covered in Lesson 7, which need no qualifying period at all — there is simply no claim to bring, however unfair the dismissal felt.

This qualifying period is currently the single most litigated threshold question in unfair dismissal practice, and it is worth being exact about it now: it is measured in continuous employment, it currently stands at two years, and it is a live area of legislative change you'll return to properly in Lesson 15 — but it is not six months yet, and treating it as though it already were is the most common error students make on this topic.

components.definition: The minimum length of continuous employment — currently two years, under s 108 ERA 1996 — an employee must have before the general right to claim unfair dismissal under s 94 ERA 1996 arises. Certain dismissals (covered in Lesson 7) are automatically unfair and require no qualifying period at all.

interaction.prompt: As the law currently stands, how much continuous service does an employee generally need before the general right to claim unfair dismissal under s 94 ERA 1996 arises?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — two years is the current, operative qualifying period under s 108 ERA 1996. The six-month figure belongs to the Employment Rights Act 2025 reform, which does not commence until 1 January 2027.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The current qualifying period is two years, not six months. The six-month figure is a reform under the Employment Rights Act 2025 that has not yet commenced — don't apply it before its start date.

parts.heading: Five doors, and only one has to open
parts.voice: reference-style — a checklist part students return to
body: Once an employee qualifies, the tribunal's inquiry has two stages, and it is essential to keep them separate. The first stage — this lesson's focus — asks only whether the employer has shown a potentially fair reason for the dismissal. The second stage — the subject of Lesson 6 — asks whether dismissing for that reason was actually fair in the circumstances. A dismissal can fail at either stage, and they are tested differently.

Section 98(1)–(2) ERA 1996 sets out a closed list of potentially fair reasons. There are five: conduct (the employee's behaviour); capability or qualifications (the employee's skill, aptitude, health or qualifications for the role); redundancy (the statutory definition covered in Lesson 8); a statutory restriction making it illegal to continue employing the person in that role (illegality); and 'some other substantial reason of a kind such as to justify the dismissal' — the deliberately open-ended fifth category, often abbreviated SOSR, which catches everything the first four don't (a breakdown in a working relationship, a business reorganisation short of redundancy, a client's insistence that an employee be removed).

Critically, s 98(1) places the burden of proof at this first stage on the employer: it is for the employer to show the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal, and that it falls within one of these five categories. An employer who cannot identify any potentially fair reason loses at this stage without the tribunal even reaching the question of fairness.

components.label: The five potentially fair reasons — s 98(1)–(2) ERA 1996
points: Conduct — the employee's behaviour, ranging from minor misconduct to gross misconduct
Capability or qualifications — skill, aptitude, health, or the qualifications required for the role
Redundancy — the statutory definition under s 139 ERA 1996 (covered in Lesson 8)
Illegality (statutory restriction) — continued employment in the role would contravene a statutory duty or restriction
Some other substantial reason (SOSR) — a deliberately open residual category, of a kind such as to justify dismissal

components.text: In determining for the purposes of this Part whether the dismissal of an employee is fair or unfair, it is for the employer to show — (a) the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal, and (b) that it is either a reason falling within subsection (2) or some other substantial reason of a kind such as to justify the dismissal of an employee holding the position which the employee held.
elements: The burden of identifying the reason sits with the employer, not the employee
The reason must be the actual, principal reason for the dismissal
It must fall within one of the four listed categories in s 98(2), or qualify as SOSR under s 98(1)(b)

interaction.prompt: Put these stages of a s 98 unfair dismissal inquiry in the correct order.
items: Confirm the employee has the qualifying continuous service to bring the claim
The employer identifies the reason (or principal reason) for the dismissal
The tribunal checks the reason falls within one of the five potentially fair categories
The tribunal moves to ask whether dismissing for that reason was fair in all the circumstances
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: qualification is a threshold gate, the reason is the employer's to establish, categorisation is the tribunal's check, and only then does the fairness inquiry — Lesson 6's territory — begin.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The order matters: qualification has to be settled before anything else, the employer must show the reason before the tribunal can categorise it, and 'was it fair' only comes after a potentially fair reason has already been established.

parts.heading: Conduct and capability: the two everyday categories
parts.voice: direct — grounds the two most-tested reasons in concrete facts
body: Conduct and capability look similar in practice — both concern something about the employee — but they are conceptually distinct, and mixing them up is a common exam slip. Conduct concerns culpable behaviour: something the employee did, and could reasonably have chosen not to do — persistent lateness, insubordination, dishonesty, harassment of colleagues. Capability concerns an employee's ability to do the job, which is not necessarily anyone's fault: poor performance despite genuine effort, a qualification the role turns out to require that the employee doesn't hold, or ill health that prevents the employee from carrying out the role.

The distinction matters because it shapes what a fair process looks like — a theme Lesson 6 develops in full. A conduct dismissal typically calls for an investigation and disciplinary process addressing culpable behaviour; a capability dismissal for poor performance typically calls for warnings, support and a genuine opportunity to improve, because the employee isn't necessarily doing anything wrong on purpose. Ill-health capability dismissals raise their own considerations, including medical evidence and, often, the duty to consider reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010 if a disability is in play — a theme picked up again in the discrimination lessons.

Illegality, the fourth category, is narrower than either: it covers situations where continuing to employ the person in that role would itself contravene a statutory requirement — the standard example is a driver whose job requires a licence being disqualified from driving. It is not a general escape hatch for 'the employer would prefer not to employ this person'; the statutory restriction must genuinely make continued employment in that role unlawful.

components.definition: Conduct concerns culpable behaviour the employee could have chosen to avoid; capability concerns an employee's actual ability, skill, qualifications or health, and does not require culpability. The distinction shapes what a fair process looks like at the second stage of the unfair dismissal inquiry.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this dismissal is best categorised as capability, not conduct.
interaction.scenarioText: Marcus has worked hard in his new sales role for six months but has consistently missed his targets by a wide margin despite coaching and support. His manager decides he simply isn't able to do the job to the required standard and dismisses him.
tappableSpans: isn't able to do the job to the required standard
interaction.correctSpan: isn't able to do the job to the required standard
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the capability framing. Marcus isn't accused of culpable wrongdoing — he tried, and was supported, but the underlying issue is ability, not behaviour he chose. That places this firmly in the capability category rather than conduct.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the language describing ability rather than blameworthy choices. Working hard despite support and still falling short describes a capability problem, not misconduct — there's no suggestion Marcus did anything culpable.

parts.heading: Redundancy and SOSR: the other two doors
parts.voice: structural — completes the five-category map before the interaction
body: Redundancy gets a full lesson of its own (Lesson 8), because it carries its own statutory definition under s 139 ERA 1996 and its own consultation duties — but as a potentially fair reason for the purposes of this stage, it is enough to know that a genuine redundancy situation (a reduced need for employees to do work of a particular kind, or workplace closure) is one of the five s 98(2) categories, and that an employer relying on it must show the redundancy situation genuinely exists.

'Some other substantial reason' is the category students tend to underrate, because it sounds like a vague catch-all rather than a real legal category — but it is used constantly in practice. Its function is to let the tribunal recognise a genuine, substantial business reason for dismissal that doesn't fit neatly into conduct, capability, redundancy or illegality. Common examples include: a business reorganisation that changes the role without amounting to redundancy in the strict statutory sense; a third party (such as a major client) refusing to work with a particular employee and giving the employer no realistic alternative; or an irretrievable breakdown in a working relationship, particularly in a small team, that makes continued employment unworkable.

SOSR is not, however, a way for an employer to dismiss for a trivial or fabricated reason and dress it up in these words — the reason still has to be substantial (not a reason that could justify dismissing an employee holding that position) and genuine, and the tribunal will scrutinise a claimed SOSR reason as carefully as any other category before moving to the fairness stage.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often treat SOSR as meaning 'any reason the employer can point to,' effectively as if the closed list in s 98 weren't closed at all.
components.whyItsWrong: SOSR still has to be substantial — of a kind capable of justifying the dismissal of someone in that position — and genuinely the reason relied on. It is a residual category for real business reasons that don't fit the other four boxes, not a general licence to dismiss for a flimsy or invented reason.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario more clearly falls within the SOSR category, rather than conduct?
interaction.scenarioA: An employee is dismissed after a major client states it will terminate a lucrative contract unless that specific employee is removed from the account, and the employer has no alternative role to offer.
interaction.scenarioB: An employee is dismissed after repeatedly ignoring explicit instructions from their manager and being rude to colleagues in team meetings.
interaction.explanation: A is a textbook SOSR situation — a substantial business reason (a client ultimatum with no realistic alternative) that isn't culpable behaviour by the employee at all. B describes culpable, blameworthy behaviour — insubordination and rudeness — which falls within conduct, not SOSR.

parts.heading: Putting the gateway together
parts.voice: reflective — closes by rehearsing the whole structure as an exam checklist
body: Bring the pieces of this lesson together and you have a two-question filter that should run automatically at the start of any unfair dismissal problem question: first, does the employee qualify to bring the claim at all (two years' continuous service, unless an automatically unfair category from Lesson 7 applies)? Second, can the employer point to a genuine reason for dismissal that falls within one of the five s 98 categories, with the burden of showing that resting squarely on the employer?

Get both of those right, and you've correctly scoped the problem before a word is said about fairness — which is exactly where Lesson 6 picks up. Get either wrong, and everything that follows is built on the wrong foundation: either you're analysing a claim that can't be brought at all, or you're testing a reason the employer never actually has to establish.

One forward pointer worth banking now, without pre-empting Lesson 15: the two-year qualifying period taught in this lesson is the current, operative rule, but it is scheduled to change. The Employment Rights Act 2025 will reduce the qualifying period to six months once that reform commences on 1 January 2027. Until that date, the two-year rule taught here is the law a tribunal will apply.

components.title: The s 98 gateway
components.description: The two-stage filter applied before an unfair dismissal claim reaches the fairness inquiry.

nodes.label: Does the employee have two years' continuous service (or fall within an automatically unfair category)?
No → no claim under the general unfair dismissal right (subject to Lesson 7 exceptions)
Yes → employer must show the reason for dismissal
No potentially fair reason shown → dismissal is unfair
Falls within one of the five s 98(1)–(2) categories → proceed to the fairness inquiry (Lesson 6)

components.textAlternative: First check qualification: two years' continuous service, or an automatically unfair category. If not qualified, there is no claim under the general right. If qualified, the employer must show the reason for dismissal. If no potentially fair reason is shown, the dismissal is unfair. If a reason is shown and falls within conduct, capability, redundancy, illegality or SOSR, the claim proceeds to the fairness inquiry covered in Lesson 6.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the six-month qualifying period is already the law a tribunal applies today?
sliderLabels: Confident it is not yet in force
interaction.explanation: Not yet in force. The Employment Rights Act 2025's reduction of the qualifying period to six months does not commence until 1 January 2027. Today's operative rule remains the two-year qualifying period under s 108 ERA 1996.

testPool.prompt: Name the current qualifying period for the general right to claim unfair dismissal, and the section that creates it.
acceptableAnswers: two years continuous employment under section 108
testPool.modelAnswer: Two years of continuous employment, under s 108 ERA 1996 — the current, operative qualifying period, unaffected until the Employment Rights Act 2025's six-month reform commences on 1 January 2027.

testPool.prompt: Which party bears the burden of showing the reason for dismissal under s 98(1) ERA 1996?
Which of the following is NOT one of the five potentially fair reasons under s 98(1)–(2) ERA 1996?
testPool.trapExplanation: 'General commercial convenience' sounds like it should fit somewhere, but it is not itself one of the five categories — a genuine business reason still has to be shown to fall within conduct, capability, redundancy, illegality or, most likely here, SOSR (and SOSR still requires the reason to be substantial, not merely convenient).

testPool.prompt: Order these events in the sequence a tribunal would consider them.
items: Check the employee's continuous service against the qualifying period
Identify the employer's stated reason for dismissal
Categorise that reason within the s 98(1)–(2) list
Assess whether dismissal for that reason was fair (Lesson 6)

testPool.prompt: Under s 98(1)(a)–(b) ERA 1996, what exactly must the employer show, beyond just naming a reason for the dismissal?
options: That the reason is the actual (or principal) reason, and falls within a s 98(2) category or qualifies as SOSR
That the reason was approved in advance by ACAS
That the employee agreed the reason was fair at the time
testPool.explanation: Section 98(1) requires two things: the reason (or principal reason) actually relied on, and that it falls within one of the listed categories or qualifies as SOSR. Naming a plausible-sounding reason that wasn't the real one, or that fits none of the categories, does not satisfy s 98(1).

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the phrase that places the burden of showing the reason for dismissal on the employer.
testPool.passage: In determining for the purposes of this Part whether the dismissal of an employee is fair or unfair, it is for the employer to show the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal, and that it is either a reason falling within subsection (2) or some other substantial reason of a kind such as to justify the dismissal.
testPool.ratioSentence: it is for the employer to show the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that means this employee cannot bring a general unfair dismissal claim under s 94 ERA 1996.
testPool.scenarioText: Rosa has worked for her employer for eighteen months. She believes her dismissal for poor timekeeping was harsh and poorly handled, and none of the automatically unfair categories apply to her situation.
tappableSpans: worked for her employer for eighteen months
none of the automatically unfair categories apply
testPool.correctSpan: worked for her employer for eighteen months
testPool.explanation: Eighteen months falls short of the current two-year qualifying period, and none of the automatically unfair exceptions apply on these facts — so, however harsh the dismissal felt, Rosa cannot bring a claim under the general s 94 right.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a capability dismissal, rather than conduct?
testPool.scenarioA: An employee is signed off with a long-term illness that medical evidence confirms will prevent him from ever safely returning to his physically demanding role.
testPool.scenarioB: An employee is caught deliberately falsifying his expense claims over several months.
testPool.explanation: A concerns the employee's actual ability to do the job — here, made impossible by ill health, with no culpability involved. B is culpable, dishonest behaviour the employee chose to engage in, which is conduct rather than capability.

testPool.prompt: An employer dismisses an employee because a key client has threatened to end a major contract unless the employee is removed, and no alternative role exists. Which s 98 category best captures this reason?
testPool.explanation: There is no culpable behaviour by the employee (ruling out conduct) and no statutory restriction making continued employment unlawful (ruling out illegality). A genuine, substantial business pressure with no alternative is the classic SOSR fact pattern.

testPool.prompt: Femi has worked for his employer for one year and eleven months. He is dismissed after his role is genuinely eliminated in a restructuring that reduces the need for employees doing his particular kind of work. Analyse whether Femi can bring a claim under the general unfair dismissal right, and, if he could, what reason the employer would need to show.
factsToOrder: Femi has one year and eleven months of continuous service
His role is genuinely eliminated in a restructuring
There is a reduced need for employees doing his particular kind of work

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Femi meets the qualifying period for the general unfair dismissal right, and, if so, what reason his employer would need to establish.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 108 ERA 1996 requires two years' continuous service for the general right under s 94; s 98(1)–(2) requires the employer to show a reason falling within one of five categories, of which redundancy — a reduced need for employees to do work of a particular kind — is one.
modelAnswer.application: Femi has one year and eleven months' service, one month short of the two-year qualifying period, and nothing on these facts suggests an automatically unfair category applies. On the facts given, he does not meet the threshold to bring a general unfair dismissal claim at all — the redundancy reason, though it would otherwise be a genuine potentially fair reason under s 98(2), never becomes relevant because the claim cannot get past the qualifying-period gate.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Femi cannot bring a general unfair dismissal claim: he falls one month short of the two-year qualifying period, so the tribunal never reaches the question of whether redundancy was a fair reason.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that 'some other substantial reason' allows an employer to dismiss for any reason it chooses, provided it names one?
sliderLabels: Confident — the reason must genuinely be substantial
testPool.correctPosition: the reason must genuinely be substantial
testPool.explanation: SOSR is a real legal category, not a blank cheque. The reason relied on must be substantial — genuinely capable of justifying dismissal of someone in that position — and it must be the actual reason, not a label attached to a trivial or invented one.

testPool.prompt: An employer dismisses a lorry driver after he is disqualified from driving by a court, since driving is an essential requirement of his role. Which category most precisely captures this reason?
options: Conduct, because the disqualification followed the employee's own driving offence
Illegality (statutory restriction), because continued employment in that specific role would now contravene the law
Capability, because the employee can no longer perform to standard
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to reach for conduct because the underlying offence was the employee's own doing, or capability because he now can't do the job — but the precise legal characterisation of the dismissal reason turns on the fact that continuing to employ him as a driver would itself be unlawful. That is illegality, a narrower and more specific category than either alternative.

testPool.prompt: Which section of the Employment Rights Act 1996 creates the right not to be unfairly dismissed?
testPool.explanation: Section 94 creates the right itself. Section 98 sets out the potentially fair reasons and the burden of showing one; section 139 is the redundancy definition, covered separately in Lesson 8.

testPool.prompt: An employee with three years' service is dismissed, and the employer cannot identify any reason for the dismissal that falls within the s 98 categories. What is the result?
options: The dismissal is unfair, because the employer has failed to satisfy the s 98(1) burden
The dismissal is automatically fair, because three years' service is well above the qualifying period

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the future six-month qualifying period as though it were already in force, or skipping the qualifying-period check altogether and jumping straight to arguing about fairness. Always run the gateway in order: qualification first, then a genuine reason within one of the five s 98 categories — fairness itself is Lesson 6.
